transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you here today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um, I guess I’m here because things have just been getting really overwhelming at work lately, and it’s starting to really affect my confidence, to be honest. I’m an auditor, and you know, in my line of work, the details are everything. You can’t just sort of do the job halfway. But what really pushed me to finally make this appointment—and I’ve been thinking about it for a while, just putting it off, you know how that goes—is that I keep starting these follow-up items after my audits. Or even after these mentorship events I run for the junior staff, which I really love doing. I sit down with every intention of finishing them. I’ll draft the email, I’ll pull up the review notes, I’ll get the forms ready, and I feel like I’m right on top of it. And then, somehow, I get distracted or I move on to something else, and I find out days later—sometimes from a partner asking me where the file is—that the final email never actually got sent, or the review note wasn't saved, or the form never actually got done. It’s so embarrassing. I mean, I’m 47 years old, I’ve been doing this for a long time, and I just feel like I should be able to finish a simple task without leaving it hanging in the wind like that. It’s just happening so much more now, and I don't know why I can't just follow through.
Outside of work, do you find yourself getting distracted or having trouble finishing tasks at home or in other daily activities?

Oh, absolutely. It’s not just the audits, it really bleeds into everything else, which is honestly just as frustrating—if not more so—because these are things I *want* or *need* to do for my own life. I mean, I forget things that I absolutely, one hundred percent mean to do. 

Like, it happens all the time with my finances, which is ironic given what I do for a living! I will get a bill in the mail, or the email notification pops up on my phone, and I think to myself, "Okay, I have the money in the checking account, I'm going to log in and pay this right after dinner." And then dinner happens, I start cleaning the kitchen, maybe the phone rings, and suddenly it's two weeks later and I'm getting hit with a late fee. Why can't I just click the button and pay the bill before the fee hits? It makes no sense. 

And it's not just bills, it happens with people and commitments, too. I’ll be driving home or making dinner, and I’ll realize I completely forgot to call a junior staff member back after I promised I would help them with a question. Or, with those mentorship events I mentioned earlier—someone will ask me to help out, I'll say yes, it sounds like a great idea, we have a whole lovely conversation about it. And then... I just never put the event on my calendar. Even after I've completely agreed to it! It just completely evaporates from my mind until someone texts me asking if we're still on for tomorrow. It makes me look so flaky, and I’m really not a flaky person, I care deeply about these things. But it’s like there’s this massive disconnect between my intention to do the thing and actually getting it done in my day-to-day life, and I just end up feeling like I'm constantly letting people down.
Do you find that your ability to focus or finish tasks is worse at certain times of the day, like in the morning when you first start your day or later in the evening?

You know, I’ve actually thought about that a lot, trying to figure out if there’s some kind of pattern to it, because if there was a pattern, maybe I could fix it, right? But honestly, I can't say it's worse in the morning or worse at night. It’s just... it’s all the time. It really is. 

Like, take the morning, for example. I’ll get up, I’ll have my coffee—I always have my coffee first thing, black, no sugar, because I read once that sugar spikes your insulin too early and causes a crash, and I definitely don't need help crashing—and I’ll sit down at my desk at home, because I work a hybrid schedule now, mostly remote since 2020. And I’ll think, "Okay, I am fresh, I am ready, I’m going to tackle this audit report before the emails start flooding in." And then I’ll open the report, but I’ll notice a notification on my phone, or I’ll remember I need to water the plants, and suddenly it’s 10:30 AM and I’ve reorganized my entire desk drawer but haven’t written a single sentence of the report. 

But then, if you look at the afternoon or the evening, it’s not any better! By the time 3:00 or 4:00 PM rolls around, I’m usually trying to wrap up, and I’ll have this burst of, "Oh my gosh, I need to get this done before I log off." And I’ll try to focus, but my brain just feels like it’s buzzing, like a television turned to static. And then after dinner, like I mentioned with the bills, I’ll sit down on the couch, totally relaxed, thinking it’s the perfect time to just do some life admin, pay the electric bill, RSVP to a wedding... and I just can't. I’ll end up scrolling on my phone or watching half a documentary about something completely random, like, I don't know, the history of the Roman aqueducts, and the bill just sits there. So, no, I wouldn't say it's a time-of-day thing at all. It’s just this constant, low-level inability to get from point A to point B, no matter what the clock says.
Do you often feel restless, as if you need to be moving or doing something, even when you’re trying to relax or focus on a task?

Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, all the time. It’s actually really funny that you ask that because, well, in auditing, obviously, you spend a lot of time just sitting and looking at screens. You really have to sit and review these massive files, sometimes hundreds of pages of ledgers or compliance notes. And when I’m doing a long review, sitting still just feels... it honestly feels physically uncomfortable. It’s not just that I’m bored with the material, it’s like there is this actual, physical pressure building up inside me. Like a soda bottle that’s been shaken up, you know? 

The longer I sit there staring at the spreadsheet, the worse it gets. I try to bargain with myself, I'll say, "Just finish this section, just get through this one account reconciliation," but the pressure just keeps mounting and mounting in my chest and my legs until I absolutely *have* to stand up. I just can't take it anymore. So I’ll get up, and I’ll walk over to the printer. And the ridiculous thing is, half the time I haven’t even printed anything! I just completely invent a reason to move. I’ll pretend I need to check if there’s paper in the tray, or I’ll walk to the kitchen to get water even though the water bottle right there on my desk is completely full. 

And it’s not just at work, either. Even when I’m trying to relax, like I mentioned before about sitting on the couch after dinner... even if I'm watching that documentary, my foot is usually bouncing, or I’m constantly shifting my weight, or I’ll suddenly decide I need to get up and fold a blanket. My husband will ask me, "Why can't you just sit and watch a movie?" but I just... I can't. The stillness is almost painful, if that makes any sense? It’s just this constant, humming need to be doing *something* with my body, even when my brain is begging for a break.
Looking back, would you say that you had trouble focusing or staying still even when you were a child, like in school or at home?

Oh, definitely. It goes all the way back to when I was just a little girl, honestly. I mean, if you were to dig up my old elementary school report cards—which my mother definitely still has saved in a memory box somewhere at her house—they all basically said the exact same thing, year after year. 

It was always this classic refrain of, "She’s such a bright girl, she's very capable," but then there was always a "but" attached to it. It was always, "but she loses her assignments," or "she rushes past the small details," which is just so incredibly ironic considering I grew up to be an auditor where details are literally the entire job. And the teachers were constantly writing these little notes to my parents about how I talked out of turn during lessons, or how I constantly needed reminders just to finish the worksheet that was sitting right in front of me. I'd just be off in my own world or chatting with whoever was sitting next to me, completely forgetting what I was supposed to be doing.

My mother actually still jokes about it to this day. We’ll be at a family gathering or something, and she’ll bring up how I could completely ace a test—like, get a perfect score on a math quiz without even trying—but then I would completely forget to turn in the big project that was literally sitting right there in my backpack. It would just be shoved in the bottom of my bag, probably getting crushed under a heavy textbook or a sweater, and I’d just have no memory of it the second I walked through the classroom door. 

It drove her absolutely crazy, because she knew I had done the work at home! We would spend the whole evening on a project, she'd watch me put it in the bag, and then... poof. Out of sight, out of mind. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing for me. It's been this exact same frustrating pattern since I was in the first grade, just playing out in different, more adult ways as I got older. It's exhausting to think about how long I've been doing this, really.
